the simultaneous adsorption and displacement of protein and nanoparticles at the air-water interface leads to a layer morphology with nanoparticles surrounded by a protein globule shell and that the layer is fragile and can be broken into separate islands by a weak mechanical perturbation.
the simultaneous adsorption at the interface of protein and silica nanoparticles leads to the formation of an interfacial layer with a high dynamic surface elasticity and fragile nature.
The surface properties of aqueous dispersions consisting of a mixture of silica nanoparticles and lysozyme were studied using surface sensitive techniques.

silica nanoparticles are adsorbed at the air/wa-ter interface in the form of protein-nanoparticle complexes.
silica nanoparticles can be coated with lysozyme to form a stable colloidal dispersion in water, which can then be deposited onto a surface.

we were able to show that the adsorption of a mixture of protein/nanocolloid complexes and free protein to an air/water interface leads to an interfacial layer of protein globules and nanocolloids, which can be easily broken into islands of irregular shape, while the adsorption of the complexes alone results in the formation of a more dense interfacial layer with much higher dynamic elasticity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the adsorption of nanoparticles in protein dispersions can lead to a significant increase in the dynamic surface properties and to the formation of a complex layer morphology.
the surface properties of protein/nanomaterials are determined by the balance between the adsorption of protein molecules and the adsorption of nanoparticles.
, in addition to the protein globules, protein/nanoparticles complexes also adsorb at the air/waters interface and contribute to the formation of an interfacial layer.
